# Matrix Patterns

The pattern of entries can reveal how a matrix behaves before any calculation

- [Diagonal matrices act one coordinate at a time](#diagonal-matrices-act-one-coordinate-at-a-time)
- [Triangular matrices expose pivots](#triangular-matrices-expose-pivots)
- [Transpose exchanges rows and columns](#transpose-exchanges-rows-and-columns)
- [Symmetric matrices mirror pairwise relationships](#symmetric-matrices-mirror-pairwise-relationships)

## Diagonal matrices act one coordinate at a time

For

$$
\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}
d_1&0&\cdots&0\\
0&d_2&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\cdots&d_n
\end{bmatrix},
$$

each coordinate is scaled independently:

$$
\mat{D}\vct{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
d_1x_1&d_2x_2&\cdots&d_nx_n
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
$$

::: {.key-point}
For a positive integer $k$, $\mat{D}^k$ has diagonal entries $d_i^k$

&nbsp;

If every $d_i\ne0$, $\mat{D}^{-1}$ has diagonal entries $1/d_i$
:::

## Triangular matrices expose pivots

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Lower triangular

$$
\mat{L}=\begin{bmatrix}
\ell_{11}&0&0\\
\ell_{21}&\ell_{22}&0\\
\ell_{31}&\ell_{32}&\ell_{33}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Zeros lie [above]{.alert} the diagonal
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Upper triangular

$$
\mat{U}=\begin{bmatrix}
u_{11}&u_{12}&u_{13}\\
0&u_{22}&u_{23}\\
0&0&u_{33}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Zeros lie [below]{.alert} the diagonal
:::
:::

- Gaussian elimination with a pivot in every row produces an upper-triangular matrix
- triangular systems are solved in order by forward or back substitution

::: {.key-point}
A triangular matrix is invertible exactly when every diagonal entry is nonzero

&nbsp;

Its inverse has the same triangular form
:::

## Transpose exchanges rows and columns

For

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}=\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\2&5\\3&6\end{bmatrix}
$$

- entries exchange positions: $(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})_{ij}=a_{ji}$
- products reverse order: $(\mat{A}\mat{B})^{\mathsf T}=\mat{B}^{\mathsf T}\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}$

::: {.key-point}
The transpose exchanges the roles of rows and columns
:::

## Symmetric matrices mirror pairwise relationships

A square matrix is [symmetric]{.alert} when

$$
\mat{S}=\mat{S}^{\mathsf T}
$$

For example,

$$
\mat{S}=\begin{bmatrix}
4&-1&2\\
-1&3&0\\
2&0&5
\end{bmatrix}
$$

has matching entries $s_{ij}=s_{ji}$ across its diagonal

- invertible covariance matrices and their precision matrices are symmetric ([Inverses]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#covariance-describes-joint-variation))
- $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\mat{A}$ and $\mat{A}\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}$ are always symmetric

::: {.key-point}
Symmetry records the same pairwise value in both directions
:::

# Elimination Becomes a Factorization

Elimination separates a matrix into simpler structured factors

Start with LU when no row exchanges are needed; then add a permutation matrix to obtain the PLU form used by SciPy

- [Inverse elimination matrices form $\mat{L}$](#inverse-elimination-matrices-form-l)
- [A permutation matrix records row order](#a-permutation-matrix-records-row-order)
- [SciPy writes $\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}$](#scipy-plu)
- [Rectangular PLU uses compact factors](#rectangular-plu-uses-compact-factors)
- [Triangular factors organize repeated solves](#triangular-factors-organize-repeated-solves)

## Inverse elimination matrices form $\mat{L}$ {#inverse-elimination-matrices-form-l}

Recall the coefficient matrix from [Systems and Matrices]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#the-augmented-matrix-stores-the-system):

$$
\mat{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&-1\\
2&-1&1\\
3&1&2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The two column-elimination stages give

$$
\mat{M}_1=
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\-3&0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{M}_2=
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&-1&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\mat{U}=\mat{M}_2\mat{M}_1\mat{A}
=\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&-1\\
0&-5&3\\
0&0&2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

---

### Undoing the stages produces $\mat{L}$

The elimination stages satisfy

$$
\mat{U}=\mat{M}_2\mat{M}_1\mat{A}
$$

Undoing them in reverse order gives

$$
\mat{A}=
\underbrace{\mat{M}_1^{-1}\mat{M}_2^{-1}}_{\mat{L}}\mat{U},
\qquad
\mat{L}=\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\2&1&0\\3&1&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Without row exchanges, elimination gives $\mat{A}=\mat{L}\mat{U}$

&nbsp;

We use this factorization without proving the general result
:::

## A permutation matrix records row order

A [permutation matrix]{.alert} is obtained by reordering the rows of the identity matrix

Write $\mat{P}_{jk}$ for one exchange of rows $j$ and $k$. In PLU, $\mat{P}$ records the combined row ordering.

$$
\mat{P}=\begin{bmatrix}
0&1&0\\
0&0&1\\
1&0&0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{P}
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_2\\x_3\\x_1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Left multiplication by $\mat{P}$ reorders matrix rows in the same pattern

Every row and column of $\mat{P}$ contains exactly one $1$

$$
\mat{P}^{-1}=\mat{P}^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
\mat{P}^{\mathsf T}\mat{P}=\mat{I}
$$

::: {.key-point}
A single row-exchange matrix is symmetric; a general permutation matrix need not be
:::

## SciPy writes $\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}$ {#scipy-plu}

If elimination uses a row reordering, then

$$
\mat{P}^{\mathsf T}\mat{A}=\mat{L}\mat{U}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}
$$

For the $\mat{A}$ below, SciPy returns the nonsymmetric $\mat{P}$ shown on the preceding slide

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
- $\mat{P}^{\mathsf T}$ places rows in elimination order
- $\mat{L}$ records elimination multipliers
- $\mat{U}$ is upper triangular
- $\mat{P}$ restores the original row order
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="false"}
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import lu

A = np.array([[0, 3, 1],
              [2, 1, 3],
              [4, 2, 2]])
P, L, U = lu(A)
np.allclose(A, P @ L @ U)       # True
np.allclose(P.T @ A, L @ U)     # True
```
:::
:::

::: {.small}
This is the convention returned by [SciPy's `lu` function](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.lu.html)
:::

::: {.notes}
Sources:

- [SciPy `scipy.linalg.lu` documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.lu.html)
:::

## Rectangular PLU uses compact factors

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$, set $k=\min(m,n)$. SciPy returns

$$
\mat{P}\in\reals^{m\times m},
\qquad
\mat{L}\in\reals^{m\times k},
\qquad
\mat{U}\in\reals^{k\times n},
\qquad
\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Wide or square: $m\le n$

- $\mat{L}$ is square and unit lower triangular
- $\mat{U}$ has zeros below its diagonal
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Tall: $m>n$

- $\mat{L}$ has $1$'s on its diagonal and zeros above it
- $\mat{U}$ is square and upper triangular
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
For a tall matrix, the compact form omits the guaranteed zero rows at the bottom of full $\mat{U}$ and the matching columns of full $\mat{L}$
:::

## Triangular factors organize repeated solves

For a square nonsingular matrix, if $\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}$, then

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\mat{L}\mat{U}\vct{x}=\mat{P}^{\mathsf T}\vct{b}
$$

Introduce $\vct{y}=\mat{U}\vct{x}$ and solve two triangular systems:

$$
\underbrace{\mat{L}\vct{y}=\mat{P}^{\mathsf T}\vct{b}}_{\text{forward substitution}},
\qquad
\underbrace{\mat{U}\vct{x}=\vct{y}}_{\text{back substitution}}
$$

::: {.key-point}
For many right-hand sides, reuse $\mat{P}$, $\mat{L}$, and $\mat{U}$; do not form $\mat{A}^{-1}$ merely to solve
:::

# Matrices as Linear Transformations

A matrix is an input–output rule that preserves linear combinations

- [A matrix maps one coordinate space into another](#a-matrix-maps-one-coordinate-space-into-another)
- [Linear transformations preserve combinations](#linear-transformations-preserve-combinations)
- [Standard basis vectors reveal every column](#standard-basis-vectors-reveal-every-column)
- [Build a standard matrix from an action](#build-a-standard-matrix-from-an-action)

## A matrix maps one coordinate space into another

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$, define

$$
T_{\mat{A}}:\reals^n\longrightarrow\reals^m,
\qquad
T_{\mat{A}}(\vct{x})=\mat{A}\vct{x}
$$

When $m=n$, $T_{\mat{A}}$ is a [matrix operator]{.alert} on $\reals^n$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Domain

$\reals^n$: the allowed inputs

Columns of $\mat{A}$ determine the input dimension
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Codomain and range

$\reals^m$: the allowed outputs

The [range]{.alert} is the subset actually reached
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Matrix size is output dimension by input dimension
:::

## Linear transformations preserve combinations

A transformation $T$ is [linear]{.alert} when

$$
T(\vct{u}+\vct{v})=T(\vct{u})+T(\vct{v}),
\qquad
T(c\vct{u})=cT(\vct{u})
$$

Equivalently, for all scalars $a,b$,

$$
T(a\vct{u}+b\vct{v})
=aT(\vct{u})+bT(\vct{v})
$$

Every matrix transformation $T_{\mat{A}}(\vct{x})=\mat{A}\vct{x}$ is linear

::: {.key-point}
Linearity forces $T(\vct{0})=\vct{0}$, so a translation $\vct{x}\mapsto\mat{A}\vct{x}+\vct{b}$ is not linear unless $\vct{b}=\vct{0}$
:::

## Standard basis vectors reveal every column

The $j$th [standard basis vector]{.alert} $\vct{e}_j$ has a $1$ in position $j$ and zeros elsewhere

Every vector is a linear combination of these vectors:

$$
\vct{x}=x_1\vct{e}_1+\cdots+x_n\vct{e}_n
$$

Therefore,

$$
T(\vct{x})
=x_1T(\vct{e}_1)+\cdots+x_nT(\vct{e}_n)
$$

For the standard matrix $\mat{A}$ of $T$,

$$
\mat{A}
=\begin{bmatrix}
T(\vct{e}_1)&\cdots&T(\vct{e}_n)
\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Every linear $T:\reals^n\to\reals^m$ has exactly one standard matrix $\mat{A}$; its $j$th column is $T(\vct{e}_j)$
:::

## Build a standard matrix from an action

Let $T:\reals^2\to\reals^3$ be

$$
T(x,y)=(x+2y,\ 3x-y,\ -x+y)
$$

The basis images are

$$
T(\vct{e}_1)=T(1,0)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
T(\vct{e}_2)=T(0,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Place them in the columns of the standard matrix:

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
T(\vct{x})=\mat{A}\vct{x}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The dimensions $\reals^2\to\reals^3$ require a $3\times2$ standard matrix
:::

# Geometry of Matrix Transformations

The images of the coordinate directions reveal the geometry

- [One vector reveals three different actions](#one-vector-reveals-three-different-actions)
- [Diagonal actions stretch and flip coordinate directions](#diagonal-actions-stretch-and-flip-coordinate-directions)
- [Reflections preserve information](#reflections-preserve-information)
- [Projections discard information](#projections-discard-information)
- [Rotation follows the basis directions](#rotation-follows-the-basis-directions)

## Diagonal actions stretch and flip coordinate directions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Stretch by different amounts

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}2x\\y/2\end{bmatrix}
$$

- horizontal distances double
- vertical distances halve
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Flip one direction

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}-x\\y\end{bmatrix}
$$

- the first coordinate reverses
- the second stays fixed
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Diagonal structure turns independent coordinate actions into one matrix transformation
:::

## Reflections preserve information

Reflection across the line $y=x$ exchanges the coordinates:

$$
\mat{H}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{H}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}y\\x\end{bmatrix}
$$

Its columns are the reflected basis vectors:

$$
\mat{H}\vct{e}_1=\vct{e}_2,
\qquad
\mat{H}\vct{e}_2=\vct{e}_1
$$

Reflecting twice restores every vector:

$$
\mat{H}^2=\mat{I},
\qquad
\mat{H}^{-1}=\mat{H}
$$

::: {.key-point}
A reflection changes geometry without losing information
:::

## Projections discard information

Projection onto the $x$-axis keeps the first coordinate and removes the second:

$$
\mat{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{Q}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}x\\0\end{bmatrix}
$$

- $\mat{Q}$ is diagonal and symmetric
- $\mat{Q}^2=\mat{Q}$: projecting again changes nothing
- every point on the vertical line through $(x,0)$ has the same image

::: {.key-point}
A projection is singular: it collapses a direction and cannot be undone
:::

## Rotation follows the basis directions

A counterclockwise rotation through angle $\theta$ sends

$$
\vct{e}_1\longmapsto
\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta\\\sin\theta\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\vct{e}_2\longmapsto
\begin{bmatrix}-\sin\theta\\\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}
$$

These images become the columns:

$$
\mat{R}_{\theta}
=\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\
\sin\theta&\cos\theta
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Rotating backward undoes the action:

$$
\mat{R}_{\theta}^{-1}=\mat{R}_{-\theta}=\mat{R}_{\theta}^{\mathsf T}
$$

# Compose and Undo Transformations

Matrix multiplication records a sequence of actions

- [Composition is matrix multiplication](#composition-is-matrix-multiplication)
- [Order can change the picture](#order-can-change-the-picture)
- [Inverse transformations undo in reverse order](#inverse-transformations-undo-in-reverse-order)
- [A factorization is a composition of simpler actions](#a-factorization-is-a-composition-of-simpler-actions)

## Composition is matrix multiplication

Suppose

$$
T_{\mat{A}}:\reals^n\to\reals^k,
\qquad
T_{\mat{B}}:\reals^k\to\reals^m
$$

First apply $T_{\mat{A}}$, then $T_{\mat{B}}$:

$$
(T_{\mat{B}}\circ T_{\mat{A}})(\vct{x})
=\mat{B}(\mat{A}\vct{x})
=(\mat{B}\mat{A})\vct{x}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The rightmost matrix acts first: $T_{\mat{B}}\circ T_{\mat{A}}=T_{\mat{B}\mat{A}}$
:::

## Order can change the picture

Let $\mat{R}$ rotate $90^\circ$ counterclockwise and let $\mat{Q}$ project onto the $x$-axis:

$$
\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Rotate, then project

$$
\mat{Q}\mat{R}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}-y\\0\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Project, then rotate

$$
\mat{R}\mat{Q}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}0\\x\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::
:::

Usually $\mat{Q}\mat{R}\ne\mat{R}\mat{Q}$; planar rotations about the same origin are a useful commuting exception

## Inverse transformations undo in reverse order

If $T_{\mat{A}}$ and $T_{\mat{B}}$ are invertible operators on $\reals^n$, then

$$
(T_{\mat{B}}\circ T_{\mat{A}})^{-1}
=T_{\mat{A}^{-1}}\circ T_{\mat{B}^{-1}}
$$

The corresponding matrix rule from [Inverses]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#undo-products-in-reverse-order) is

$$
(\mat{B}\mat{A})^{-1}
=\mat{A}^{-1}\mat{B}^{-1}
$$

- rotations are undone by rotation through the opposite angle
- reflections are undone by the same reflection
- projections have no inverse because they lose information

::: {.key-point}
Undo the last action first
:::

## A factorization is a composition of simpler actions

The PLU factorization

$$
\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}
$$

describes the action of $\mat{A}$ as a sequence:

$$
\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{U}\ }
\mat{U}\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{L}\ }
\mat{L}\mat{U}\vct{x}
\xrightarrow{\ \mat{P}\ }
\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}\vct{x}
=\mat{A}\vct{x}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Factorization is representation by simpler actions; multiplication composes them
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- Special matrix [patterns reveal behavior]{.alert} before computation
- In SciPy's convention, elimination gives $\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}$
- A [linear transformation]{.alert} preserves combinations; basis images determine its standard matrix
- Reflections and rotations are reversible; projections [discard information]{.alert}
- In a product, the [rightmost transformation acts first]{.alert}
- Inverses undo compositions in reverse order

# What Comes Next

Matrix transformations can

- stretch or shrink regions
- preserve or reverse orientation
- flatten a plane into a line

[Determinants]({{< meta decks.d04.file >}}) will attach one number to a square matrix action and answer:

- By what factor does area or volume change?
- Is orientation preserved or reversed?
- Has a dimension collapsed?

::: {.key-point}
Next: [measure how a matrix transformation scales and orients space]({{< meta decks.d04.file >}}){.alert}
:::
